'''Cécile Andrée Paule DeWitt-Morette''' (21 December 1922&nbsp;– 8 May 2017) was a French mathematician and physicist. She founded the [[Les Houches School of Physics]] in the [[French Alps]]. For this and her publications, she was awarded the American Society of the French [[Legion of Honour]] 2007 Medal for Distinguished Achievement.<ref name=legion/> Attendees at the summer school included over twenty students who would go on to be Nobel Prize winners,<ref name="dyk"/> including [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]], [[Georges Charpak]], and [[Claude Cohen-Tannoudji]], who identify the school for assisting in their success.<ref name=senior/>

==Biography==

=== Early life and education ===
Cécile Morette was born in 1922<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Cécile Andrée Paule DeWitt-Morette|encyclopedia=Women in Chemistry and Physics: A Biobibliographic Sourcebook|publisher=Greenwood Press|author=DeWitt, Bryce|editor1=Grinstein, Louise S. |editor2=Rose, Rose K.|editor-link1=Miriam Rafailovich |editor3=Rafailovich, Miriam H. |year=1993|pages=150–161}}</ref> and brought up in [[Normandy]], where in 1943 she earned her License des Sciences from the [[University of Caen]].

Despite her original intention to become a surgeon,<ref name="UT Physics: Cecile DeWitt-Morette">{{cite web|url=http://www.ph.utexas.edu/person/dewitt_cecile|title=UT Physics: Cecile DeWitt-Morette|accessdate=30 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141013204139/http://www.ph.utexas.edu/person/dewitt_cecile|archive-date=13 October 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> she completed her degree in mathematics, physics, and chemistry due to limited opportunities to attend medical school in France during [[World War II]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/UTexas_Physics_History/Cecile_DeWitt-Morette.html|title=UT Physics: Cecile DeWitt-Morette|accessdate=30 October 2014|archive-date=17 October 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017063556/http://www.ph.utexas.edu/utphysicshistory/UTexas_Physics_History/Cecile_DeWitt-Morette.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ph.utexas.edu/person/dewitt_cecile|title=UT Physics History: Cecile DeWitt-Morette|accessdate=30 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141013204139/http://www.ph.utexas.edu/person/dewitt_cecile|archive-date=13 October 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Following the completion of her bachelor's degree, Morette entered the [[University of Paris]]. She was studying there when her mother, sister, and grandmother were killed in the [[Battle_for_Caen|Allied bombing]] of [[Caen]] to support the [[D-Day]] landings.<ref name="UT Physics: Cecile DeWitt-Morette"/> In 1944, while still working toward her doctorate at the University of Paris, Morette took a job at the [[Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique]] (CNRS), then under the direction of [[Frédéric Joliot-Curie]].<ref name="UT Physics: Cecile DeWitt-Morette"/> She worked as a scholar at the [[Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies]] from 1946 to 1947. In 1947, she completed her Ph.D. (''Sur la production des mésons dans les chocs entre nucléons'').<ref name=works>[https://web.archive.org/web/20120304082152/http://godel.ph.utexas.edu/Members/cdewitt/pubsCecile.pdf List of publications], University of Texas, accessed 2015-04-19</ref><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=45835}}</ref>

=== Career ===
In 1948 she was invited to the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] (IAS) in [[Princeton, New Jersey]] by [[Robert Oppenheimer]],<ref name=senior/> who had recently become director of the institute.<ref name="IAmBecome">{{cite news|title='I Am Become Death...': The Agony of J. Robert Oppenheimer|author=Rhodes, Richard|authorlink=Richard Rhodes|work=[[American Heritage (magazine)|American Heritage]]|date=October 1977|url=http://www.americanheritage.com/articles/magazine/ah/1977/6/1977_6_70.shtml|accessdate=23 May 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060507095756/http://www.americanheritage.com/articles/magazine/ah/1977/6/1977_6_70.shtml|archive-date=7 May 2006|url-status=dead}}</ref> While there, she became interested in [[Richard Feynman]]'s [[Path-integral formulation|path integral formulation]] for computations in quantum mechanics and worked to make this approach rigorous, which ultimately led to wide applications of the [[Feynman diagram]]s and the underlying mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/startswithabang/2017/06/20/from-wartime-devastation-to-academic-discrimination-cecile-dewitt-morette-overcame-it-all/|title=From Wartime Devastation To Academic Discrimination, Cecile DeWitt-Morette Overcame It All|last=Halpern|first=Paul|date=June 20, 2017|website=Forbes|language=en|access-date=2019-02-09}}</ref> She also met her future husband and scientific collaborator, American physicist [[Bryce DeWitt]] while at IAS; the couple married in 1951, and would have four children.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Oral History Transcript: Drs Bryce DeWitt & Cecile DeWitt-Morette|work=American Institute of Physics|accessdate=19 April 2015|date=28 February 1995|url=http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/23199.html|archive-date=13 January 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150113021118/http://www.aip.org/history/ohilist/23199.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

To revitalize French research in mathematics and physics following the war, DeWitt-Morette established a summer school, [[Les Houches School of Physics]], at [[Les Houches]] in the [[French Alps]]<ref name="houches">{{cite web|url=https://translate.google.com/translate?hl=en&sl=fr&u=http://houches.ujf-grenoble.fr/&ei=e3ufS86hFMyK4gbp4LWXDg&sa=X&oi=translate&ct=result&resnum=1&ved=0CAsQ7gEwAA&prev=/search%3Fq%3DL%2527Ecole%2Bde%2BPhysique%2Bdes%2BHouches%2Baccueille%26hl%3Den%26rlz%3D1C1GGLS_en-GBGB366GB366|title=L'Ecole de Physique des Houches (English translation)|language=French|accessdate=16 March 2010}}</ref> in 1951. She told stories of how she obtained the funding by tricking her way into a minister's office and then persuaded her male colleagues to support the idea by pretending that the idea was theirs.<ref name=senior>[https://www.seniorwomen.com/articles/articlesIntCecile.html Cécile DeWitt-Morette profile], seniorwomen.com; accessed 18 June 2015.</ref>

Morette was to lead this school for the next 22 years. The school was able to list twenty former students or lecturers at the school who went on to become [[Nobel laureates]].<ref name="dyk">{{cite journal|date=July 1999|title=The School High in the Alps|journal=Europhysics News|publisher=Springer Berlin/Heidelberg|volume=30|issue=3|page=68|issn=1432-1092|doi=10.1007/s007700050127|doi-access=free}}</ref> The French mathematician [[Alain Connes]], who is a recipient of the [[Fields Medal]], credited the summer school as responsible for his career in mathematics. Nobel laureates [[Pierre-Gilles de Gennes]], [[Georges Charpak]], and [[Claude Cohen-Tannoudji]] identified the school as helping with their success.<ref name=senior/> In 1958, [[NATO]] funded a series of advanced study centres that were based on Morette's summer school.<ref name="houches"/> In 1987, Cecile DeWitt-Morette participated in a Quantum Gravity Seminar in Moscow together with her husband.<ref>Alexei B. Gaina, Some forgotten relativists,15th Marcel Grossmann Meeting, Rome 2018 [http://dbserver.icra.it:8080/mg15/pdf/HR1-598GA679EI.pdf]</ref>

Bryce DeWitt died in 2004 from cancer. In 2007, DeWitt-Morette was awarded the American Society of the French Legion of Honour 2007 Medal for Distinguished Achievement in New York. She was then the Jane and Roland Blumberg Centennial Professor Emerita of Physics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name=legion>[http://www.ph.utexas.edu/news.html Department of Physics News] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100609104302/http://www.ph.utexas.edu/news.html |date=2010-06-09 }}, University of Texas at Austin; accessed 18 June 2015.</ref>

==Work==
In 1951, she independently developed a formula to calculate path integrals. This is now known as the Van Vleck–Pauli–Morette formula, named after [[John Hasbrouck Van Vleck]], [[Wolfgang Pauli]] and her.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kleinert |first=Hagen |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/Path_Integrals_in_Quantum_Mechanics_Stat/d4Sp6zqhPP8C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=pauli+morette+formula&pg=PA348&printsec=frontcover |title=Path Integrals in Quantum Mechanics, Statistics, Polymer Physics, and Financial Markets |date=2004 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-238-107-1 |language=en}}</ref>

In 1953 a trustee of the unusual [[Gravity Research Foundation]], [[Agnew Hunter Bahnson]], contacted Bryce DeWitt with a proposal to fund a gravity research institute. The proposed name was agreed as the "Institute for Field Physics" and it was established in 1956 at the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]] under the direction of Bryce and Morette.<ref>[http://cwp.library.ucla.edu/Phase2/DeWitt-Morette,_Cecile@862345678.html Profile], cwp.library.ucla.edu; accessed 18 June 2015.</ref> Under the Institute of Field Physics DeWitt-Morette and her husband organized the [[Chapel Hill Conference]] on gravitation in 1957.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Rickles |first=Dean |url=https://edition-open-sources.org/sources/5/index.html |title=The Role of Gravitation in Physics: Report from the 1957 Chapel Hill Conference |last2=DeWitt |first2=Cécile M. |date=2011-02-14 |publisher=Max-Planck-Gesellschaft zur Förderung der Wissenschaften |isbn=978-3-945561-29-4 |series=EOS – Sources |location=Berlin |language=en}}</ref> "She was an instructor in the department from 1956-1971 but was offered a position at the University of Texas at Austin after UNC failed to promote her despite her significant contributions to physics and the department. The DeWitts then left together with their students in January of 1972."<ref>{{Cite web |title=Section III |url=https://physics.unc.edu/home/department-history/section-iii/ |access-date=2023-08-28 |website=Department of Physics and Astronomy |language=en-US}}</ref>  

In 1958 Cécile DeWitt-Morette invited [[Léon Motchane]] to see the [[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute of Advanced Study]] in USA<ref>{{cite web|last=DeWitt-Morette|first=Cécile|title=1948–1950: Snapshots|url=http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/ias-letter/articles/2011-spring/ias-dewitt-morette|publisher=[[Institute for Advanced Study|Institute of Advanced Study]]|access-date=2013-05-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130522063958/http://www.ias.edu/about/publications/ias-letter/articles/2011-spring/ias-dewitt-morette|archive-date=2013-05-22|url-status=dead}}</ref> which inspired [[Léon Motchane]] to establish an institute dedicated to fundamental research in three areas: mathematics, theoretical physics, and the methodology of human sciences upon which he later created the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]].<ref name="The IHÉS at Forty">{{cite web|last=Jackson|first=Allyn|title=The IHÉS at Forty|url=https://www.ams.org/notices/199903/ihes-changes.pdf|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|accessdate=April 19, 2015}}</ref>

===Expedition to test general relativity===
In 1972 Morette and her husband led an expedition to [[Mauritania]] to confirm that light was deflected in line with the theory of [[general relativity]], to improve on [[Arthur Eddington]]'s [[Eddington experiment|1919 experiment]]. These measurements were made during the [[solar eclipse]] there. Comparison of the pictures with those made six months later confirmed that, in line with theory, light was indeed bent when passing by massive objects.<ref>[http://www.maa.org/features/010906jan_archives.html Archives of American Mathematics Spotlight: The Bryce S. DeWitt Papers], Kristy Sorensen, accessed March 2010</ref> Morette and her husband joined the faculty of the University of Texas in 1972. She began to work increasingly in physics rather than in mathematics, and she became a Professor in 1985.<ref name=senior/>

==Awards and honours==
In 2007 Professor Cécile DeWitt-Morette was awarded the American Society of the French Legion of Honour 2007 Medal for Distinguished Achievement in New York. She was then the Jane and Roland Blumberg Centennial Professor Emerita of Physics at the [[University of Texas at Austin]].<ref name="legion"/>

In 2026, DeWitt-Morette was announced as one of 72 historical women in STEM whose names have been proposed to be added to the [[List of the 72 names on the Eiffel Tower|72 men]] already celebrated on the [[Eiffel Tower]]. The plan was announced by the Mayor of Paris, [[Anne Hidalgo]] following the recommendations of a committee led by [[Isabelle Vauglin]] of [[Femmes et Sciences]] and Jean-François Martins, representing the operating company which runs the Eiffel Tower.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Eiffel Tower: a list of 72 women scientists will soon be inscribed on the Parisian monument |url=https://www.sortiraparis.com/en/news/in-paris/articles/340564-eiffel-tower-list-of-72-women-scientists-soon-to-be-honored-on-the-paris-landmark |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=www.sortiraparis.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2026-01-26 |title=Eiffel Tower to honor 72 women scientists for posterity |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/france/article/2026/01/26/eiffel-tower-to-honor-72-women-in-science-for-posterity_6749828_7.html |access-date=2026-02-09 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Les noms des 72 femmes pour la Tour Eiffel ont été révélés. |url=https://www.femmesetsciences.fr/news/les-noms-des-72-femmes-pour-la-tour-eiffel-ont-%C3%A9t%C3%A9-r%C3%A9v%C3%A9l%C3%A9 |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=Femmes & Sciences |language=fr}}</ref><ref>[https://10ca8303-b3dc-4a91-9dcc-2d2b91792b47.usrfiles.com/ugd/10ca83_3838bd19a41a4e83927cfc8fe0f50404.pdf 72 femmes de sciences pour la tour Eiffel] ''Femmes & Sciences'' (in French). Retrieved 2026-02-09</ref>
